\chapter{The Actor and the Actress}
\label{ch:actor-actriz}
\hlchaptermodality{421}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the actor and the actress, say why the feminine is actriz rather than actora, and ask who is in a film rather than only what the film is.}

Ask who is in the film and answer with a person rather than a thing, choosing the article from the person's gender and not from the word's ending.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el actor]{el actor — the one who does, which is all the word has ever meant}

\label{lesson:ES-C421-actor}



\begin{quote}
You can name \emph{el teatro} and \emph{la película}. Say both. Now say the one thing neither of them can do without, and that you have never been given a word for.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el teatro — the looking-place, where this person works in front of you.
  \item la película — the film, where this person works on a strip of plastic instead.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{stress-final} — \emph{ac-TOR}, stress on the last syllable. English says \emph{AC-tor} and Spanish says the opposite end. Moving it is the whole difference between sounding Spanish and sounding foreign here. $\to$ reference
  \item \texttt{r-tap} — the final \textbf{r} is one flick of the tongue, not the English curl.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el actor} — \textquotedblleft{}the actor.\textquotedblright{} Latin \textbf{actor}, from the verb \textbf{agere}, \textquotedblleft{}to drive, to do, to set in motion.\textquotedblright{}

Latin built agent nouns with \textbf{-tor}: take a verb, add \emph{-tor}, and you get \emph{the one who does it}. The pattern is still visible in dozens of English words that were borrowed whole:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Latin verb} & \textbf{meaning} & \textbf{the one who does it} \\
\midrule
agere & to do & \textbf{actor} \\
docere & to teach & doctor \\
dirigere & to direct & director \\
inspicere & to look into & inspector \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So \emph{actor} is not a theatre word at all. It is \textbf{doer}, and Latin used it for anyone who acted in any sense — an agent, a driver of cattle, a man pleading a case in court. The stage borrowed a perfectly ordinary word and kept it.

\emph{Agere} is still visible all over English, and it never stopped meaning \textquotedblleft{}do\textquotedblright{}: an \textbf{agent} is someone doing something on your behalf, an \textbf{agenda} is literally \emph{things that must be done}, and an \textbf{action} is a doing.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the two workplaces}]
The same person, two places you already have words for:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{where} & \textbf{what is watched} & \textbf{live?} \\
\midrule
el teatro & the actor & yes \\
el cine & la película & no \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{El actor} is masculine and takes \emph{el}. That is the easy half. The other half — what to call a woman who does the same work — is the next lesson, and Spanish answers it with an ending that almost nothing else in the language uses.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el actor\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ac-TOR}, stress at the end
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el actor del teatro\textquotedblright{} — the actor from the theatre
  \item which English word meaning \textquotedblleft{}things to be done\textquotedblright{} comes from the same Latin verb (\emph{agenda})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{agere} mean? (To do, to drive.) So what does the \emph{-tor} ending add? (The one who does it.) Where does the stress fall in \emph{actor} in Spanish? (On the last syllable: \emph{ac-TOR}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la actriz]{la actriz — the ending that did not follow the usual rule}

\label{lesson:ES-C421-actriz}



\begin{quote}
You have \emph{el actor}. Say it. Now guess the feminine before reading on, and expect to be wrong — the obvious guess is not what Spanish does here.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el actor — the doer, from \emph{agere}, with the Latin agent-noun ending \emph{-tor}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{stress-final} — \emph{ac-TRIZ}, stress on the last syllable, like \emph{actor}. $\to$ reference
  \item \texttt{r-tap} — the \textbf{r} in \emph{-triz} is a single tap, and it sits between two consonants, which is where it is easiest to over-roll.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la actriz} — \textquotedblleft{}the actress.\textquotedblright{} Not \emph{la actora}, which is what the ordinary Spanish habit of swapping \textbf{-o} for \textbf{-a} would have produced.

Latin had its own feminine for \emph{-tor} nouns: \textbf{-trix}. \emph{Actor} / \textbf{actrix}. Spanish inherited that pair intact, turned the Latin \textbf{-x} into \textbf{-z}, and kept it.

The ending is nearly extinct. Spanish has only a small handful of \emph{-triz} words left, and they are worth seeing together because the list is short enough to hold in your head:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{masculine} & \textbf{feminine} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
el actor & la \textbf{actriz} & the actor \\
el emperador & la empera\textbf{triz} & the emperor \\
el institutor & la institu\textbf{triz} & the governess \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English kept the same Latin ending in \textbf{aviatrix} and \textbf{dominatrix}, and in the mathematical \textbf{matrix} — originally \emph{mater} plus \emph{-trix}, \textquotedblleft{}the womb\textquotedblright{}, the thing from which other things are produced.

Everywhere else in Spanish, the feminine of a person-noun is the ordinary swap: \emph{el camarero} / \emph{la camarera}. \textbf{-triz} is the exception, and \emph{actriz} is the one you will meet most.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two words, one root, three endings}]
Everything on this row came out of one Latin verb:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{ending} & \textbf{what the ending does} \\
\midrule
\textbf{act}o & — & the deed itself \\
el \textbf{act}or & -or & the man who does it \\
la \textbf{act}riz & -riz & the woman who does it \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Strip the endings and the same three letters are left standing: \textbf{act-}. The root does the meaning; the ending only says \emph{who}.

Note the article changes with the person, not with the building: \emph{el actor del teatro}, \emph{la actriz del teatro}. The theatre stays masculine either way.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}la actriz\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ac-TRIZ}, stress at the end
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el actor y la actriz\textquotedblright{} — and hear that only the article and the ending moved
  \item \textquotedblleft{}la actriz del teatro\textquotedblright{}
  \item the feminine of \emph{emperador}, using the same ending (\emph{emperatriz})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why is it not \emph{la actora}? (Spanish inherited the Latin feminine \emph{actrix} whole, rather than applying its own \textbf{-o} to \textbf{-a} swap.) Which English word for a grid of numbers carries the same ending? (\emph{Matrix}.) Which syllable is stressed in both \emph{actor} and \emph{actriz}? (The last.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la escena completa]{la escena completa — two places, one thing, two people}

\label{lesson:ES-C421-repaso-escena}



\begin{quote}
Name the two people from the last two lessons, with their articles, before reading further.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: places, things and people take different endings}]
Five words, and the gender of each is decided by a different kind of evidence:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{article} & \textbf{what decides it} \\
\midrule
el teatro & el & the \textbf{-o} ending of a place-word \\
el cine & el & inherited with the shortened word \\
la película & la & the \textbf{-a} ending of a thing-word \\
el actor & el & the person is male \\
la actriz & la & the person is female \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That is the useful split. For a \textbf{place} or a \textbf{thing}, the ending tells you the article and the world has no say in it. For a \textbf{person}, the world decides and the ending follows.

So \emph{la película} is feminine for a reason that has nothing to do with anyone being female, while \emph{la actriz} is feminine for exactly that reason.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
Read this aloud. Every word in it has appeared before:

\begin{quote}
El actor está en el teatro. La actriz está en el cine. La película es de la actriz.
\end{quote}

Three short sentences, five known words, no new grammar.
\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the two places with \emph{el} (\emph{el teatro}, \emph{el cine})
  \item the thing with \emph{la} (\emph{la película})
  \item the two people, each with its own article (\emph{el actor}, \emph{la actriz})
  \item which of the five is feminine because a person is female, and which is feminine only because of its ending
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two of the five change their article according to who is being talked about? (\emph{El actor} and \emph{la actriz}.) Which three never change? (\emph{El teatro}, \emph{el cine}, \emph{la película}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[¿Quién está en la película?]{¿Quién está en la película? — the question the two new words were for}

\label{lesson:ES-C421-sintesis-espectaculo}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{el actor} and \emph{la actriz} once each. You are about to use both inside a question rather than on their own.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: naming a person answers a different question}]
Two question words you already have, pointed at the same film:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{question} & \textbf{what it asks for} & \textbf{answer from this chapter} \\
\midrule
¿Qué es? & a thing & \emph{Es una película.} \\
¿Quién está en la película? & a person & \emph{El actor.} / \emph{La actriz.} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Qué} wants the thing word. \emph{Quién} wants the person word. Until this chapter you could answer only the first of the two about anything on a screen or a stage, because the corpus had named the film and never named anyone in it.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
\begin{quote}
— ¿Vamos al cine? — Sí. ¿Qué película es? — Es la película de la actriz. — ¿Y el actor? — El actor está en el teatro.
\end{quote}

Note the inverted marks opening each question, and that \emph{de la actriz} is how Spanish says \emph{the actress's}.
\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}¿Quién está en la película?\textquotedblright{} and then answer it with each of the two people in turn
  \item \textquotedblleft{}la película del actor\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}la película de la actriz\textquotedblright{}, and hear where \emph{de + el} contracts and where it cannot
  \item where each of the two people is, using \emph{el teatro} and \emph{el cine}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which question word asks for a person rather than a thing? (\emph{Quién}.) What happens to \emph{de el} in \emph{la película del actor}? (It contracts to \emph{del}.) Why does \emph{de la actriz} not contract? (The contraction exists only for \emph{de + el}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
